#9947. Announcing AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered intelligence to optimize your cloud environment (preview)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the public preview of AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. The AWS Well-Architected Agent analyzes your infrastructure, understands unique business goals, and delivers contextual recommendations with ready-to-implement fixes. It delivers context-aware optimization without relying on manual audits or generic checklists.

The agent evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would. It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.

Here are the three main features of this service:

AWS Well-Architected Agent in action To get started, create an agent profile to define the scope of what Well-Architected Agent can access and provide recommendations on, complete the IAM role setup to access resources, conduct architecture review, and remediate recommendations.

Create an agent profile In the AWS Well-Architected console, choose Get started with Well-Architected Agent. You can define an agent profile that specifies which AWS accounts and applications to monitor, which optimization pillars to focus on, and the permissions required.

You can choose AWS accounts or AWS Regions to monitor and optimization pillars that matter most to your business. You can also set goals for each pillar: cost optimization, performance, resilience, and security.

To give access to the agent for your AWS environment, provision customer-managed IAM roles the agent uses to read resource configurations, utilization metrics, and application topology. To learn more, visit the IAM prerequisite for AWS Well-Architected Agent.

When you choose Get Started, the agent creates your agent profile. Resource and application recommendations will be generated within 24 hours after profile creation.

You can conduct an architecture review on pre-deployment workloads by uploading an IaC project in Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) to be analyzed. Choose Conduct architecture review in the dashboard, upload a.zip file containing IaC project or repository file, and select which Well-Architected lens to use for reviewing your infrastructure.

You can define your applications to add context which will enhance the relevancy and further contextualize recommendations. Choose Add application context in the dashboard, add your applications with AWS accounts, AWS Regions, AWS services, tags if you want to narrow the scope to specific resources, and the details of applications.

Review prioritized recommendations and start remediating Now you can see generated prioritized recommendations generated by the agent across your resources and applications, selected pillars, ranked against your declared goals, with automation-ready remediation included.

When you choose the specific recommendation, you can see the details, insights into why the agent are suggesting the recommendation, impacts and trade-off, and recommended fixes across affected AWS resources.

Choose Start remediation to address recommended fixes. You can choose the console, updated IaC template, CLI commands to remediate by the resolution type. It provides detailed step-by-step instructions and you can roll out this instruction and verify the result.

When you choose Using updated IaC template, the agent provides the code changes needed to update your existing IaC templates such as the CDK function shown above which you can copy directly into your codebase.

You can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the AWS Well-Architected Agent documentation.

Things to know Here are some things that you should know about the Well-Architected Agent.

You can still use existing AWS Well-Architected Tool to manually evaluate your cloud architecture with user-defined lenses that measure your workload using your own best practices.

Join the preview Access to the AWS Well-Architected Agent and its recommendations is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). You can onboard workloads from any AWS commercial Region. AWS Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and available to AWS customers with an AWS Support plan.

Give it a try today in the AWS Well-Architected console and send feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#9945. DevFest is back!

Technology is evolving at a breakneck speed—from generative AI and autonomous agents, to scalable cloud infrastructure and modern web standards. What better way to stay connected, than to roll up your sleeves, experiment, and build alongside a thriving global community at your local DevFest.

Build, Secure and Scale in the Agentic Era

DevFest is the world’s largest, annual, community-led event series aimed to educate developers and builders about Google’s latest technologies. Hosted by Google Developer Groups (GDG), DevFest will run from October 1 through December 31, 2026. Across 800+ global events, almost 1 million attendees will gather across 115 countries, to connect and learn how to build, secure, and scale in the agentic era.

Through interactive sessions and workshops, Devfest will deep dive into the latest Google AI technologies and also offers comprehensive tracks for Google Cloud, Android and Web, giving every developer and builder actionable tools to deploy real-world solutions.

#9944. Dev error bricked 600 PCs, caused $1M CD-ROM write-off

One lucky engineer scored a free dinner during the frantic fix, the rest got to explain their mistake

Welcome to Monday, the day upon which The Register offers a new instalment of "Who, Me?" – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of messing up, 'fessing up, and somehow finding redress.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Oriel" who told us he once worked for a vendor of small business accounting software.

This story comes from a time when software shipped on CD-ROMs and users bought it off the shelf in actual shops. The vendor released a new version each year and always shipped it before a major holiday that's celebrated with a giant meal.

Oriel was part of the team whose job it was to get the package ready on time.

In the previous year, they flubbed the job because the program didn't always install itself on some PCs running Windows 95 or Windows ME machines system due to registry corruption.

"We wanted to increase our successful installation metrics, so in conjunction with the installation team, a key decision was made – by me – to force the updating of registry keys to enable the install," Oriel admitted. In his email to The Register, he asked the portentous question: "What could possibly go wrong?"

What went wrong was that not long after the software was shipped, the vendor's support lines started getting calls from customers who complained that after installing the accounting package none of their other software would work.

"Installing a new version of our application had borked the customer's machine completely," Oriel wrote.

The company decided the best thing to do was to tell affected customers they should go and buy a new PC – and that it would pick up the bill, no questions asked.

"In the week prior to the holiday, we replaced over 600 machines," Oriel told The Register.

Oriel and his developer colleagues were of course told to fix the problem but couldn't reproduce it nor figure out their mistake.

"To get a reproduction case we need a user's machine where the user had created a Windows Registry restore point prior to installing our application," Oriel explained. If the developers could find such a machine, the plan was to roll it back to the restore point, verify everything was in order before the customer installed the update, install the accounting software, and figure out the problem.

The company tasked its support agents with finding a customer willing to surrender their PC, which proved difficult because few bothered to create a registry restore point.

The day before the holiday, a customer volunteered their machine.

This customer was located a few hours away by road, so an engineer got the job of visiting on the morning of the holiday to pick up the stricken machine, give the customer a shiny new system and configure it to their specifications.

Said engineer did the job, which took so long he was invited to stay for the holiday meal, then returned to HQ with the broken box.

The next day, Oriel and his colleagues got to work and found a fix, then created a version of the accounting application that wouldn't break any more PCs.

Oriel was, of course, summoned into a meeting with senior execs to explain the situation and watched as they decided the best course of action was to pull buggy CDs from stores – which meant trashing CDs and packaging valued at $1 million.

Have you made a mistake that broke customers' kit, or cost millions? If so, don't make the mistake of not sharing your story with The Register and click here to email the column. ®

#9940. All the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon Prime Day 2026 was exclusively for Prime members and ran June 23–26, 2026 with millions of deals across more than 35 categories.

As part of our annual tradition of sharing how AWS powered Prime Day (2016, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025), I want to share the services and chart-topping metrics from AWS that made your amazing shopping experience possible.

Prime Day 2026 – all the numbers As always, Prime Day was powered by AWS. Here are some of the most interesting and/or mind-blowing metrics:

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and AWS Graviton – During Amazon Prime Day 2026, AWS Graviton powered up to 49% of the Amazon EC2 compute used by Amazon.com.

Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon EBS, our high-performance block storage service, peaked at over 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving over an exabyte of data daily.

AWS Lambda – AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) and Fargate – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, representing a 47.7 percent increase from the previous year’s Prime Day average.

Amazon CloudFront – Amazon CloudFront delivered over 2.1 trillion HTTP requests during the global week of Prime Day 2026, a 5 percent increase in total requests compared to Prime Day 2025.

Amazon DynamoDB – Amazon DynamoDB, a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database, powers multiple high-traffic Amazon properties and systems including Alexa, the Amazon.com sites, and all Amazon fulfillment centers. Over the course of Prime Day 2026, between June 23 and June 26, 2026, DynamoDB processed over 59 trillion requests. DynamoDB maintained high availability while delivering single-digit millisecond responses and peaking at 192 million requests per second.

Amazon Aurora – On Prime Day, Amazon Aurora, a relational database management system (RDBMS) built for high performance and availability at global scale for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and DSQL, processed hundreds of billions of transactions, stored 5,491 terabytes of data, and transferred 1,194 terabytes of data.

Amazon ElastiCache – During Prime Day, Amazon ElastiCache peaked at serving over 2.3 quadrillion daily requests and 2.1 trillion requests in a minute.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams – Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, a fully managed serverless data streaming service, processed a peak of 988 million records per second during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) – Amazon SNS, a fully managed pub/sub messaging service for application-to-application and application-to-person communication, delivered 5 trillion messages in a single day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) – Amazon SQS, a fully managed message queuing service for microservices, distributed systems, and serverless applications, received a peak of 213 million messages per second during Prime Day 2026

AWS CloudTrail – AWS CloudTrail processes billions of API activity events per day for governance, compliance, and operational auditing. During Prime Day 2026, that volume surged to 3.6 trillion events in just four days, a 44% increase over Prime Day 2025.

Amazon CloudWatch – Amazon CloudWatch processed over 2.15 quadrillion metric observations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon GuardDuty – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon GuardDuty monitored an average of 14.08 trillion log events per hour, a 59% increase from last year’s Prime Day.

AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) – We ran over 44,000 AWS FIS experiments – more than six times what we conducted in 2025 – to help ensure Amazon.com remains highly available on Prime Day.

#9939. Memory crunch makes refurbished kit look a lot less secondhand

Soaring component costs and warranties of up to three years give buyers more reason to consider pre-loved hardware

Rising memory prices are pushing more customers toward refurbished tech, suppliers say, with warranties of up to three years helping to make secondhand kit a less daunting purchase.

Memory costs have more than quadrupled this year as manufacturers prioritize more lucrative high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for servers powering AI datacenters.

Many enterprises are keeping equipment longer in an uncertain economy. Ben Caddy, senior analyst at Omdia, said suppliers were linking refresh discussions with opportunities to recover value from customers' aging kit.

By 2030, he predicted, 35 percent of "all the hardware sold for the channel will be taken back by partners," driven "by the sheer economic logic of taking equipment back, recovering value, and embracing more circular IT lifecycles."

This is already helping some customers "unlock some capital to put towards those [relatively] small refresh plans," he said while hosting a panel on circular IT at last month's Canalys Forums in Barcelona.

Refurbished smartphones are growing in popularity, but persuading customers to trade in their old devices remains a constraint on supply.

The same applies to PCs and other equipment, said Jon Sansom, MD at GreenSafe IT. "Availability is a challenge," he said.

Marcel Joosten, group director of marketing and digital commerce at tech lifecycle specialist XTENTEC, said the company now offers trade-ins when customers buy new kit. "We're actually financing the residual value" at the end of year two, three, or four, when customers return the equipment, he told the audience.

XTENTEC collects, refurbishes, rents, and resells equipment, and has an agreement with HP to renovate aging products, with a two or even three-year warranty available as "just an SKU on the list from HP."

Joosten said equivalent support, including HP Care Pack services, helped make refurbished equipment more attractive to buyers.

Customers want to cut their carbon footprint, and many public and private sector tenders require it. But the "most important thing" for many is trust, said Patrick Molberg, CEO of Advania Finance.

"The customers have to trust the refurbished equipment and have to trust the process. And I think one of the things that we have to be better at as a whole is that we kind of need to have a standard methodology regarding verification."

Work on verification standards with vendors including HP, Lenovo, and Dell is ongoing, Molberg said. He also argued that lifecycle services should be built into purchasing decisions rather than added three or four years later.

Joosten argued that listed US tech companies' focus on quarterly sales and market share can work against refurbishment. "That needs to change," he said. "I think there should be a market share figure for circularity." ®

#9936. Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels

Per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep climbing. Price per million tokens isn't the metric that actually governs production economics anymore. The dominating metric is now cost per successful task: total spend across every loop iteration, tool call, retry and internal thinking pass divided by the number of tasks that pass verification.

When an agent calls a high-thinking reasoning configuration for every micro-decision in its harness, you're paying deep-reasoning prices for questions a lightweight configuration already answers accurately. To prevent this unnecessary overhead, consider adding a lightweight routing layer that can intercept routine decisions before they ever reach an expensive reasoning model.That is the premise behind wiring TypeSafe's Jev classifier in front of Google Antigravity's model calls. Rather than generating text token by token, Jev—a specialized structured-output classifier designed for high-throughput decision pipelines—evaluates structured classification primitives in a single forward pass: a Choice from a list, a numeric Score or a Noul, which returns a 0 to 1 probability for a binary statement.

For full disclosure, Google has no partnership with TypeSafe, and this article is not an endorsement of TypeSafe or its products. Jev is used here as one example of a lightweight classifier, and the same routing pattern can be built with other classifiers, including Google-native ones. The Getting started with discriminative models codelab, for example, runs the same kind of classifier on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, in your own Google Cloud project.

We ran a 50-question, auto-graded, coding-agent benchmark against live Gemini and Jev APIs to test whether a near-free classifier can route each task to the cheapest model that still gets it right. Here's what we learned:

The naive way to ask Jev to route a coding task is a single broad Choice question: simple or complex. When we tested that first on 16 coding-agent tasks, Jev routed nearly everything to simple, even tasks requiring an LRU cache trace or modular exponentiation. TypeSafe's documentation warns against this exact anti-pattern. If a question weighs multiple factors or requires a meta-judgment, decompose it into an atomic check.

When we replaced the broad Choice question with one atomic Noul question, it fixed the separation immediately. The question was: does answering this require performing more than one sequential calculation, simulation step or logical deduction, rather than a single direct lookup, format check or one-step classification?

On those initial 16 tasks, Jev routed 13 of 16 in agreement with our hand-labeled difficulty on the first run and 14 of 16 on the second pass. Many engineering teams ask whether they even need a classifier API when they can write a zero-cost regex and prompt-length heuristic in Python, matching words like sequence, modulo and race condition or escalating any prompt over 35 words.

On the 16 development questions used to write those exact rules, the local heuristic scored 15 of 16, or 93.8%. To test whether that heuristic survived contact with realistic coding-agent traffic, we froze its code without changing a character and added 34 unseen held-out tasks across seven coding-agent buckets: fact extraction, schema validation, short classification, single-hop code checks, state simulation traces, math or logic chains and subtle language-semantics bugs.

On the 34 held-out questions, the frozen heuristic dropped 23.2 percentage points to 70.6%. Realistic simple tasks such as extracting a port from a Kubernetes YAML manifest, a file path from a unified git diff header or a line number from a Python traceback exceeded 35 words and triggered false escalations. Conversely, concise multi-step code traces such as mutable default arguments across calls, Python dictionary key hashing on {1: "a", True: "b", 1.0: "c"} and C short-circuit evaluation lacked the heuristic's hardcoded puzzle words and were falsely routed to the simple path. Jev classified all 34 unseen tasks with 100.0% agreement, 34 of 34, reaching 48 of 50, or 96.0%, across the full suite.

A common mistake when building a fast-path router is assuming that setting a low maxOutputTokens cap on a reasoning model will make it spend less on easy tasks. Our 50-question data shows why that assumption fails.

When we compared gemini-3.8-flash with maxOutputTokens=300 against gemini-3.8-flash with maxOutputTokens=4096 while leaving thinkingConfig at the API default, both configurations spent almost identical thinking tokens on the 27 tasks Jev labeled SIMPLE:

Note: Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.

Capping the model's output at 300 tokens didn't save any money on easy tasks. The cap is only a ceiling, and easy answers never came close to it. On the easy tasks, the capped version actually cost slightly more than the uncapped one. All the cap did was break 7 of the 25 hard tasks. On six of them, the model ran out of room while still reasoning and never gave an answer. On the seventh, it squeezed its reasoning to fit, finished on time and got the answer wrong.

So a Jev router that sends easy tasks to the capped model and hard ones to normal Flash got all 50 right. It still cost slightly more than skipping the router and using normal Flash for everything, and it was slower. If your cheap option doesn't actually make the model think less on easy tasks, no router can save you money. Not even a perfect one that costs nothing.

The obvious way to spend less on thinking is to ask the model to think less. So we ran a second round of tests with two lighter options: Flash-Lite, which doesn't think at all by default, and Gemini 3.8 Flash with its thinking level set to low. We added those results to the same results file, matched question by question.

A note on timing. Most of the router's time per task is spent in Flash-Lite and Flash calls, which we measured in the same run and time window as the plain Flash baseline, so the speed comparison between them is fair. Jev's own decision is a small share of the total and comes from the first round. Speed comparisons against default Flash or Pro mix the two rounds, so read those as approximate.

Note: Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.

The 7-bucket breakdown shows where gemini-3.5-flash-lite and the heuristic router missed tasks and how Router Jev: Flash-Lite to 3.8 LOW recovered 100% accuracy:

The strongest setup without a router was Gemini 3.8 Flash on low thinking. It solved all 50 tasks. That's the number a router had to beat.

The Jev router beat it. It sends every task to Flash-Lite first and escalates only what Jev flags as complex. It also solved all 50 tasks, and it can help reduce both cost and response time compared with running low thinking on everything. On prompts this short the cost difference per task is small, so for an interactive agent the shorter wait is the bigger benefit.

Why it works. On its own, Flash-Lite answered every simple task in half a second but missed 6 of the 25 hard ones. Jev flagged all 6 as complex with high confidence and escalated them. That brought its cost close to what a perfect router would achieve.

The keyword heuristic was cheaper, but only because it got things wrong. It sent 5 hard tasks to Flash-Lite, and 2 of them failed, for 48 of 50.

Escalating to a heavier setting didn't pay here. Routing hard tasks to Flash on default thinking was cheaper than running default thinking everywhere. It still cost more than running low thinking on everything, which already solved all 50. A heavier escalation target only makes sense when the low setting starts failing.

Limits: one run per setup, 50 prompts with hand-assigned difficulty and simple automatic grading.

Two things in our results only show up once you look past it.

Routing and caching pull in opposite directions. Our test prompts were short, standalone tasks, and on those the Jev router helped reduce both cost and response time. Real coding agents often look different. They send the same big block of context on every turn, such as a map of the repository and the tool definitions. Agent Platform Context Caching stores that block so you pay 75% to 90% less to resend it. The catch is that a cache belongs to one model. If your agent switches between Flash-Lite and Flash from turn to turn, it either keeps two caches or loses the discount. The practical split: route short, self-contained tasks like log parsing or schema checks, and keep long, context-heavy turns on one model.

Match the model to the workload. Gemini 3.1 Pro is built for deep, multi-step reasoning, and it brings that same depth to every request, including short lookups that don't need it. For a workload made mostly of quick checks and extractions, a Flash configuration is the better fit, and Pro is best saved for the tasks that need its reasoning depth. Model configurations can also apply different safety settings to security-related prompts. In our run, the Pro configuration declined two short code-security review prompts that Flash answered. If your agent performs security reviews, test those prompts on the configuration you plan to use.

Other ways to build the router. Jev is one way to get a fast classifier, but not the only one. The Getting started with discriminative models codelab runs the same Choice, Score and Noul questions on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, hosted on a Compute Engine GPU VM or on Cloud Run in your own Google Cloud project. An open-source server exposes the same API in front of it, so the routing code in this article only needs a different endpoint. Our results come from Jev, so measure accuracy and latency on your own tasks before switching, and keep in mind that a self-hosted model is billed by the GPU-hour rather than by the token.

Taken together, the results give three practical rules.

Start with Flash on low thinking before you build a router. It solved all 50 tasks and cost considerably less than the default setting. Lowering the output token limit is not a substitute, because it doesn't reduce how much the model thinks on easy tasks. Set the thinking level directly, with thinkingLevel: "LOW".

Use Jev to route short, standalone tasks. Send simple tasks to Flash-Lite and hard ones to Flash on low thinking. Ask Jev one simple yes-or-no question per factor. In our test, this helped reduce cost and response time compared with running Flash on low thinking for everything, and came close to what a perfect router would achieve. Keep long, context-heavy turns on a single model so caching keeps working. For high-volume warehouse workloads, Jeff Nelson's BigQuery and Cloud Run cascade pattern applies the same idea.

Measure what your agent actually spends. Send your agent's traces and thinking-token counts to Cloud Logging and BigQuery, so you can see which tasks drive your spend and catch truncation or retries that inflate it. The benchmark code will be published after open-source review.

In summary, the most cost-effective way to run an agent is to match each task to the model that fits it. Start with a fast model on a light setting. You'll often find it already gets the job done. Then add a small, almost free classifier like Jev to send only the hard tasks to a stronger model, and ask simple yes-or-no questions rather than one broad one. Judge every option by what it costs per task done right, not per token.

#9935. AI Slop FM radio experiment puts machines on trial, one dodgy tune at a time

Music fan from Wales lets listeners pit AI-generated songs against human bops – including toilet operas and HR protest songs

A Welsh music enthusiast has built an internet radio station that plays AI-generated tunes alongside human-made tracks without telling listeners which is which, to find out whether listeners really hate AI music or just the idea of it.

AI Slop FM is the creation of Mike Chaffin, who built and runs the station single-handedly from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire. By stripping away artist names, cover art, and any mention of AI, Chaffin hopes to find out what listeners really think when they have nothing but the music to go on.

The free 24/7 station asks listeners to rate tracks from S to E, tag how the music makes them feel, and leave written feedback. The most popular submissions will eventually make it into a weekly chart called the Slop 40, giving creators something that can be hard to come by in the age of streaming: an actual audience.

Anyone can submit a track, including human musicians, although Chaffin has already discovered that not all of them are particularly keen on the idea. He told The Register that he had floated the idea to an unsigned musician friend who had sold around 600 albums, but was met with a rather nervous response.

"Wh, wh, why would I want to do that?" the musician reportedly asked, according to Chaffin, who said he had never heard his friend stutter before.

"It seems that there is a deep rooted fear of AI music in the industry," Chaffin said.

The station is still in beta, with Chaffin waiting for enough submissions to fill its schedule across different genres before opening it fully. He's already been pleasantly surprised by the quality of the music submitted, although he still listens to every track to make sure nobody is trying to pass off Bohemian Rhapsody as their own work.

Among the early offerings are what Chaffin describes as a developing genre of slightly rude protest songs about HR departments, along with an operatic epic about a blocked toilet.

"Some of which are hilarious," he said of the HR songs. As for the toilet opera, it "runs through my head about once a day, whether I like it or not."

Chaffin believes the sheer volume of music uploaded to streaming platforms means plenty of perfectly decent tracks never find an audience, whether a person or a machine made them. He hopes AI Slop FM will give some of those overlooked creations a chance to be heard.

"You don't have to have published your creations to upload. Just to own the rights," he explained.

Tracks that don't make the Slop 40 could still get another outing, with plans for genre-specific stations offering unsuccessful submissions a second chance.

The bigger question is what happens when listeners start rating AI-generated music more highly than the human competition, but Chaffin isn't particularly worried about that.

"If the machines win then their creators clearly deserve to be heard, deserve an audience. If the musicians win, then that's reassuring for them."

He also wants to see how the station's eventual top five or top ten compares with the official music charts, although with submissions having only recently opened, there are no results to pore over just yet.

"Everyone has an opinion on music before a note has been heard, by the genre, the label, the name or the cover art," Chaffin said. "We strip all that away, tracks are judged purely on the music."

Whether listeners ultimately prefer human musicians or their algorithmically assisted rivals remains to be seen. Either way, somewhere in Carmarthenshire, an opera about a blocked toilet is proving rather difficult to flush from its listener's memory. ®

#9934. Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

Lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

Let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

The only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.

Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:

Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

Better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:

For pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

He advises executives, engineers, and architects at every step along their journey to the cloud, with a deep focus on sustainability and practical design. In his free time, Micah enjoys the outdoors, photography, and chasing his kids around the house.

#9932. Portal breach at Germany's top university exposes every registered user's password

Stolen sysadmin credentials enabled a follow-on attack on the campus management system

Attackers stole central university login passwords belonging to everyone registered with the Technical University of Munich's myTUM portal, including an admin whose credentials were then used to attack a second system.

TUM restored access to its TUMonline campus management system on Monday morning, allowing users to change their passwords.

The university disclosed the attack on November 6. The initial attack targeted the myTUM portal, which serves students and faculty members, providing centralized online access to services and documents.

TUM said the attackers used the admin's credentials to launch a follow-on attack on TUMonline, its central campus management system, which forced the IT team to take it offline.

The university has not disclosed how the attackers initially gained access or how the stolen passwords were stored. It did not immediately answer questions about the number of affected users.

It also did not specify whether this sysadmin had multi-factor authentication (MFA) switched on, but it confirmed that "user accounts with MFA were protected from this attack."

Attackers may also have accessed names, home addresses, and dates of birth. Potentially exposed employee records included work addresses and phone numbers, while student records included ID numbers, degree programs, and completed semesters.

"The attackers' access within TUMonline was largely logged," said Dr Alexander Braun, CIO at TUM, in the disclosure. "After analyzing these logs, we currently assume that no other data from TUMonline was compromised, such as grades or college applications. We are continuing to investigate this."

TUM is directing users to reset their passwords through Microsoft 365 where possible. Those without MFA already configured must instead use a German electronic ID or request a reset email while connected to the campus network.

The university also warned users to watch for phishing and fraud, and to change any passwords reused elsewhere.

TUM ranks first in Germany and 25th worldwide in the QS university rankings. The STEM-focused institution reports 51,954 students across its German campuses and TUM Asia in Singapore, plus 12,850 employees. ®

#9931. PP-OCRv6 on Hugging Face: 50-Language OCR from 1.5M to 34.5M Parameters

Evaluate PP-OCRv6 online, then integrate lightweight, production-ready OCR with PaddlePaddle, Transformers, or ONNX Runtime backend.

PP-OCRv6 is the latest generation of PaddleOCR’s universal OCR model family. It is designed for real-world text detection and recognition across documents, screenshots, multilingual images, digital displays, industrial labels, and scene text.

The model family scales from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, with three tiers: tiny, small, and medium. The medium and small tiers support 50 languages, including Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages. Try PP-OCRv6 online quickly: PP-OCRv6 Online Demo.

On PaddleOCR’s official in-house multi-scenario OCR benchmarks, PP-OCRv6_medium reaches 86.2% detection Hmean and 83.2% recognition accuracy. Compared with PP-OCRv5_server, it improves text detection by +4.6 percentage points and text recognition by +5.1 percentage points.

PP-OCRv6 focuses on a practical OCR need: producing accurate, structured text outputs with small models and flexible deployment options. For a deeper discussion of why specialized OCR models remain useful in the VLM era, see our previous blog: PP-OCRv5 on Hugging Face: A Specialized Approach to OCR.

PP-OCRv6 introduces architecture, training, and data improvements across detection and recognition. The main design goal is to improve OCR accuracy while keeping model sizes suitable for different deployment settings.

PP-OCRv6 provides three model tiers, covering different model sizes and OCR accuracy levels.

PP-OCRv6 uses PPLCNetV4 as a unified backbone for text detection and text recognition.

For developers, the main benefit is consistency across the model family. The tiny, small, and medium tiers are not unrelated models; they are part of the same OCR family and share a common architectural direction.

Text detection is the first stage of the OCR pipeline. Detection quality affects the crops sent to the recognizer, and poor crops often lead to poorer recognition.

PP-OCRv6 upgrades the detection module with RepLKFPN, a lightweight large-kernel feature pyramid network designed for multi-scale text detection while keeping inference efficient.

This is relevant for real-world OCR inputs, where text may be small, dense, rotated, low-resolution, or embedded in complex backgrounds.

For text recognition, PP-OCRv6 uses EncoderWithLightSVTR. It combines local context modeling with global attention to improve recognition quality on challenging text crops.

The recognition improvements are especially relevant for multilingual text, screen text, industrial characters, special symbols, dense text, and noisy image regions.

The medium and small tiers support 50 languages in one model family, covering Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages.

This helps reduce the need for separate OCR models across common multilingual OCR scenarios.

Run OCR with Paddle Infernece(Default backend):

The OCR result can be saved as visualization images and structured JSON output. The structured output can then be used by downstream systems such as document parsing, search, extraction, RAG, analytics, or agent workflows.

PP-OCRv6 can be used with multiple inference backends through PaddleOCR. PaddleOCR 3.7 provides a unified inference-engine interface, where engine selects the underlying runtime and related configuration can be passed through the pipeline or module API.

For Hugging Face users, PaddleOCR supports running selected OCR and document parsing models with a Transformers backend. This can be enabled with:

For more details on how the Transformers backend works in PaddleOCR, see:

PaddleOCR: Running OCR and Document Parsing Tasks with a Transformers Backend

Run PP-OCRv6 example with Transformer Backend:

ONNX variants are also available in the PP-OCRv6 Collection for environments that use ONNX Runtime through engine="onnxruntime":

Together, these backend options make PP-OCRv6 available across different runtime environments while keeping the same OCR model family on the Hugging Face Hub.

PP-OCRv6 extends PaddleOCR with a lightweight, multilingual OCR model family for real-world text detection and recognition.

The release includes three model tiers from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, up to 50-language OCR support, improved detection and recognition accuracy over PP-OCRv5_server, and multiple model formats on the Hugging Face Hub, including safetensors, Paddle inference models, and ONNX models.

Together with the hosted Hugging Face Space and the available PaddleOCR inference backends, PP-OCRv6 provides several entry points for evaluation and integration:

Transformers Backend Blog: PaddleOCR with Transformers Backend

PaddleOCR Documentation: PP-OCRv6 Documentation

PaddleOCR Official Website: https://www.paddleocr.com

You can evaluate PP-OCRv6 with the online demo, explore the available model assets in the Collection, and use the inference backend that matches your own OCR workflow.

#9930. AWS Weekly Roundup: Prime Day 2026 by the numbers, Claude Haiku 5.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, and more (October 13, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning.

#9929. AI echo chambers and sanity in tech leadership: Three case studies

Altman, Torvalds, Yen. One has got his head screwed on. The others could do with some grounding

"AI delusion" remains loosely defined, but most of us know it when we see it: exaggerated faith in the technology's power, applicability, or nature, coupled with a refusal to acknowledge its limitations.

It's bad in the individual, as when an elderly relative emails you a hallucination-laden ChatGPT summary. It's worse in management, when your boss insists that AI slop is genius marketing content at a bargain rate. It is terrifying in tech CEOs. It is not, thankfully, compulsory.

Consider three recent examples of technology leadership in the age of AI. One would be Pythonesque were the disconnect with engineers and the public not so profound. Another risks becoming a business-school case study in how to demolish customer trust. The third offers something less fashionable: robust pragmatism. Saving the best till last, y'all.

Case 1: we present for your consideration Sam Altman of OpenAI, one of the few actually at the controls of the singularity machine. It seems churlish to pluck just one luscious fruit out of that cornucopia of choices, yet we must. Sam Altman thinks it is a sin against the natural order that so much RAM is idling in machines owned by individuals, organizations, and anywhere that isn't Big AI. It's oh so inefficient. How convenient that the efficient allocation of scarce resources should favor the business he runs. Free market schmarket.

Altman has since said his remarks were taken out of context and that he wants consumers to have as much memory as they like. The efficiency argument still reveals whose priorities come first.

This is the best kind of delusion, one with an undeniable truth at its core – memory does indeed get used far more intensively in AI model makers and inference servers than in your laptop. For a business selling the future, treating privately owned hardware as an inefficient allocation of resources has a distinctly Soviet flavor, and the American right has vowed to stamp out socialist extremism. Get on with it, chaps, you've only got two years left. That Altman can't see this is the best bit of the misconception.

There are two potential root causes of this Marxist-Leninist-Altmanism. One is that he's mathed the math and worked out that the only way OpenAI can hit the numbers is if it gets every last byte in the world, hot off the fab. The other is that you can't run on-prem on an 8 GB state-mandated Chromebook, and on-prem is otherwise going to twist his melon until it falls off.

Case 2: Andy Yen, CEO of Proton, the company behind Proton Mail and Proton VPN. You, me, and the household cat know ProtonMail as the secondary email that's worth paying for. You want the best recovery backup email for Gmail, you want it as an accessible end-to-end encrypted email service. You want it because it is all about stable spotless security, all about the end users, all about being there when you absolutely need it. It is safe to recommend, and you do.

Or rather that's what you thought about ProtonMail et al until the same day you learned about Andy Yen's alleged behavior. Leaked comms reported by 404 Media allege Yen saw Proton as a company that must make its numbers come what may, and one path to do that was to AI-code at maximum velocity.

Engineers who wanted to test the results for security were losers – fax machine operators in the internet age – and he didn't want them, or so the report claimed. No more engineers, just product managers in a Claude terminal. He allegedly imparted this vision through aggression, belittling employees in front of their peers, and swinging his big ol' reinterview job chopper.

More generally, running a toxic workplace should lead to instant dismissal and loss of license to be in charge of anything more sentient than a sausage machine. That AI is involved is not AI's fault. Misunderstanding the brand and the customer base so, so badly – that's the delusion.

Putting velocity of coding above that is arrant stupidity. Nobody cares. Unless new features and products increase security, they'll only matter outside the niche, where one might argue that Proton products cannot compete. Not knowing that, has the potential to destroy a brand overnight. Yen wouldn't be the first CEO to cause a company some trouble by revealing what they really think, but this one matters. Things are being rowed back – no more reinterviewing to prove allegiance to AI at all costs, and an employee has said it's not quite as bad as all that.

Case 3: Linus Torvalds. He reports that AI-based kernel code has not saturated the production pipeline, is useful when treated properly, and the kernel cadence is expanding following a stabilization period. The high-pressure AI patch spigot turned on; the appropriate plumbing was created to regulate and filter; and he is much happier now.

It's a nuanced story, and nuance is so often a dirty word in the industry. Torvalds' happiness is not a guarantee that everything in the garden is in fact lovely, but the Linus vibe is as good as any – and it's better than most predictive metrics. He is hitting his numbers, which are the quality of the code and the speed at which changes match what users need in a changing world. The numbers do not involve margins, profits, shareholder value, or driving massive investment before the gig's up.

Put another way, Torvalds has managed the arrival of AI to probably the most important codebase ever, and he has done it with, not in spite of, the most diverse and independently minded dev team that ever came through the merge window, and it's barely news. If only they gave Oscars for this sort of thing.

There is no better advert for sanity, nor for FOSS's unique and infinitely valuable ability to remain responsive to market forces without market dependency. Freedom cures delusion. Even AI delusion. It's a helluva drug. ®

#9928. Experimenting with the proposed Cross-Origin Storage API in Transformers.js

(This is a guest post by Developer Relations Engineer Thomas Steiner from the Chrome team at Google.)

Transformers.js provides Web developers with a simple way to use the power of transformers in their Web apps through task-specific pipelines. To run inference in the browser, developers create an instance of pipeline() and specify a task they want to use the pipeline for. As a concrete example, the following snippet shows how to set up an automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipeline.

You will notice in the source code that I specified Xenova/whisper-tiny.en as the model, which is a very decent choice for common English automatic speech recognition tasks. In fact, it's even the default model according to the Transformers.js default model resolution, as per the linked excerpt.

When you run this example in the browser, Transformers.js automatically takes care of downloading and caching the relevant model resources and Wasm files. The following screenshot shows the Chrome DevTools Cache storage section after visiting the app. When you reload the page, the resources are served from the Cache API, and the model returns results almost instantly.

However, Xenova/whisper-tiny.en being a popular model (and, as mentioned before, even being the ASR default model in Transformers.js), you can well imagine that more than just one app that you visit would use it. To simulate this situation, here's the same example app from before, but served from a different origin. When you visit this different origin app, rather than being usable almost instantly, the browser instead has to download and cache all the model resources again, even if they're byte-by-byte the same as before. Even in this toy example, this adds up to 177 MB of duplicate download and storage, as you can examine in the Storage section of the Chrome DevTools Application panel. You can imagine that this quickly adds up.

But it gets worse. Let's add a second pipeline to the toy example: sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis by default uses the Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english model. By not specifying the model, Transformers.js' default model resolution automatically picks it for you.

Two entirely different AI models, but they depend on the same 4,733 kB ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm WebAssembly (Wasm) runtime file from the underlying ONNX Runtime library that Transformers.js is built on top of. Open the extended demo on a different origin, and you will notice in the Network tab how also the Wasm runtime gets downloaded and cached again.

So even if you run apps that don't share the same AI models, your browser still makes redundant requests for shared Wasm resources you already have, and on top of that also caches them again, which consumes space on your hard disk.

By default, AI model resources come from the Hugging Face Hub, and ultimately the Hugging Face CDN. The browser makes a request for a resource like https://huggingface.co/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/resolve/main/config.json which then gets redirected to the final CDN URL like https://huggingface.co/api/resolve-cache/models/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/0b6928efcb76139cae2c6881d49cda67fe119f42/config.json?%2FXenova%2Fdistilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english%2Fresolve%2Fmain%2Fconfig.json=&etag=%223c36342ef1f74de2797d667c68c6b7b988d0b87c%22 in this case.

The Wasm runtime resources are served from the jsDelivr CDN by default. For example, ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm comes from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm at the time of this writing.

The concrete implementation may vary by browser, but in Chrome, cached resources are keyed using a Network Isolation Key in addition to the resource URL. The Network Isolation Key is composed of the top-level site and the current-frame site. Take the previous toy examples hosted on the origins https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. If they both use the Wasm runtime from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm, their cache keys will look like in the following table.

So even if the resource URLs are exactly the same, since the Network Isolation Keys don't match, there's no cache hit, which means duplicate download and duplicate storage. This is the challenge that the Cross-Origin Storage proposal aims to tackle.

💡 Note: The Cross-Origin Storage API is an early-stage proposal that isn't final. While the proposed API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow.

The proposed Cross-Origin Storage (COS) API introduces a dedicated navigator.crossOriginStorage interface through which web apps can store and retrieve large files across origin boundaries, identified not by a URL, but by a cryptographic hash.

That last point about cryptographic hashes is key. Because COS identifies files by their hash rather than by their URL or origin, the same ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm Wasm runtime you downloaded while visiting https://googlechrome.github.io is recognized as identical to the one https://rawcdn.rawgit.net is about to request, no matter where either of the two origins fetched it from. See the following code snippet that illustrates the basic flow.

If the resource is in COS, you get back a FileSystemFileHandle from which you can read the blob directly via getFile() (the resulting File inherits from Blob). If the resource is not in COS, you fall back to the network, and write the resource into COS for the next app that needs it, which could be your app, or another unrelated app, potentially on a completely different origin.

The API is deliberately shaped after the File System Standard's FileSystemDirectoryHandle.getFileHandle() you likely are familiar with from the Origin Private File System (OPFS) API. The hash parameter plays the same role as the name parameter in OPFS: uniquely identifying a resource. The options.create flag works the same way: absent or false for read-only access, true when you intend to write.

Not every resource should be globally shared. COS gives developers precise control over visibility through the origins option when storing a file.

One important rule: visibility can be upgraded but never downgraded. If a file is already globally available, a later attempt to store it with a restricted origins list is silently ignored. This prevents a malicious actor from re-storing a public resource and narrowing its availability. The reverse is possible: a file initially stored with a restricted origins list can later be made more permissive. Any site, not just the original storer, can call getFileHandle() for the same hash (hashes are not a secret) with create: true and a broader origins value, and given the browser verifies the hash matches, the resource becomes available to the wider audience from that point on. Note that the upgrading site must still write the full file through the returned handle. This requirement exists to prevent sites from exploiting the upgrade path as a side-channel to detect whether a particular file was already stored in COS.

A subtle but important property of COS is that the browser verifies the hash when you write a file. If the data you write doesn't match the declared hash, the write fails with an error. This makes integrity checking automatic: an app reading a file from COS can be confident it's getting exactly the bytes it expected. The same guarantee it would have had if it had computed the hash itself after a network download.

This turns out to be doubly useful in the Transformers.js scenario. Today, after downloading model weights, most apps have no practical way to verify that the CDN served the right bytes. With COS, every file in the store is implicitly verified on write, no matter where it came from, the official Hugging Face CDN or a random site's self-hosted mirror.

Of course a cross-origin shared cache raises the same question as the partitioned HTTP cache in reverse: if any site can probe for the presence of a file by hash, couldn't an attacker learn something about the user's browsing history by checking whether, say, a game engine Wasm module is cached?

COS addresses this through two complementary mechanisms:

Crucially, this means an error is not a definitive answer. It might mean "not stored", or it might mean "stored, but the browser isn't telling you". Apps should always handle it the same way: fall back to the network.

Going back to the toy examples from before: the ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm runtime weighs in at 4,733 kB and is shared by every Transformers.js-powered app regardless of which AI model it uses. With COS, the first app to load it downloads it once and stores it under its SHA-256 hash with origins: '*'. Every subsequent app, whether on https://googlechrome.github.io, on https://rawcdn.rawgit.net, or any other origin, finds it in COS immediately. The 177 MB of duplicate Whisper model weights? Same story: Xenova/whisper-tiny.en gets downloaded once, recognized by hash the second time around, and served from COS in milliseconds. And of course, the same also happens for Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english.

Transformers.js itself is already piloting the COS API at the library level. Pull request #1549 introduced an experimental COS cache backend behind an opt-in flag. Enabling it takes a single line before you set up your pipeline:

Note the experimental_ prefix on the flag. It's intentional and signals that the underlying browser API has not yet been standardized and may change without a major version bump. With that flag set, Transformers.js resolves the SHA-256 hash for each Xet-tracked model file (the large ONNX weight files) by fetching the raw Xet pointer (example raw pointer file) and extracting its oid sha256: field. It then uses that hash as the key for navigator.crossOriginStorage. If the model is already in COS (because another site stored it there first), it's served instantly without a network round-trip. If not, it falls back to a regular download and stores the result in COS for the next caller. With the toy example, the advantage in practice is that Xenova/whisper-tiny.en and Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english (and of course ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm) only ever need to cross the ether once, regardless of how many different origins ask for them.

The toy example works just fine with Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, but of course you possibly wouldn't say no if the user already has any of the other Whisper variants in their COS cache. For example, the user might already have Xenova/whisper-large-v3, which, as the name suggests, is a lot larger than the tiny variant. Transformers.js's Model Registry makes being flexible about your models possible. If you know your app's needs can be addressed by, for example, any of Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, whisper-medium.en, or Xenova/whisper-large-v3, you can check the registry for the associated files for each model, probe for their existence in the COS cache (which may partially or completely contain the model resources you need), and then take a decision what model to choose eventually. The ModelRegistry.is_pipeline_cached() API directly integrates with COS (and of course the Cache API), so this operation is really ergonomic.

The COS API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, but you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow. Check out the source code of the extension and follow the usage instructions to get started.

With the extension installed, try the full end-to-end experience right now: open the first toy example with COS enabled, let it load Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, then open the toy example with COS enabled from the second origin. Instead of the 177 MB re-download you saw before, the model is served from COS in milliseconds. When you open the extension's popup window, you can see COS in action. If you View by Resource, you can see the resource with the SHA-256 hash 950978b1dbcbf250335358c1236053ba19a7f7849b33dc777f4421b72b7626fa shared across https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. It may not be obvious, but as you can verify by comparing the SHA-256 hash on Hugging Face, you're looking at https://huggingface.co/Xenova/whisper-tiny.en/blob/main/onnx/decoder_model_merged.onnx. For now, the extension is mostly aimed at power users like you. Once implemented in the browser, there will be a friendlier integration in the browser's Settings page. The screenshot below shows the extension's popup window with the View by Resource tab active, where you can see the shared resource with its hash and the two origins that have it in their COS cache.

If you're building your own Transformers.js app, the call to action is simple: add env.experimental_useCrossOriginStorage = true before your first pipeline() call, install the extension, and watch the duplicate downloads disappear from your Network tab. Every site that opts in makes the experience faster and cheaper for every other site's users. Opting in is completely risk-free: if the COS API isn't supported because the user doesn't have the COS extension installed, the code just falls back to the default path (the Cache API).

Transformers.js is not alone in experimenting with COS. WebLLM (opt-in, see documentation) and wllama (automatic, see PR) are likewise excited about this proposed API.

On the Chrome team, we're considering implementing the COS API natively in the browser. As an early stage proposal, we welcome feedback on the API, and the shape of the proposal itself. The Cross-Origin Storage repository is the place to file issues, express support, or open PRs.

#9927. Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

Why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:

The integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

Analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

Vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:

Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where users upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

Combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

Using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a new AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

Pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Join the conversation If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Share your feedback on AWS re:Post for Amazon S3.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.
