#9881. France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns

The 'first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory'

France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.”

The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4).

The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers.

This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers.

The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers.

“The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.”

Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons.

First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says.

It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.”

In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C).

Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America.

The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.”

This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador.

However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

#9880. Hugging Face Models on Foundry Managed Compute

At Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

On top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a plan built on the H100 family today carries forward as new hardware generations come online.

Hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with new frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:

The catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means new versions and patches land on Foundry quickly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a new model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run."

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:

Each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

Hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. For a deep dive on Foundry Managed Compute — pricing, accelerator SKUs, data residency, enterprise readiness, observability, and the full Responses API + memory pattern — see the Managed Compute launch blog.

#9879. On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.

This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:

Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?", and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

With inference running locally on a paired phone, the same experience works standalone on a phone and extends naturally to hands-free smart glasses. To see how we adapted Language Teacher for intelligent glasses check out our recent talk at Android Dev Summit: Building Audio-First Experiences for Intelligent Eyewear with Gemini Nano.

Beyond the XR Language Teacher showcase, we also built ASR and TTS directly into Google AI Edge Gallery’s main AI Chat feature, giving on-device SLMs like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 a natural, offline voice interface while on the go.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

While multimodal models like Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly, we provide a modular solution for cascading language models with separate, lightweight voice models for latency optimization and flexibility. Depending on your target devices and model requirements, our open-source code on GitHub shows you the optimized and recommended solution for Android using ML Kit, as well as MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform coverage and open model support.

For developers building for Android devices, ML Kit’s GenAI Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech APIs provide a standardized, platform-integrated path out of the box. With the underlying speech models managed through AICore and Google’s on-device speech services, developers get production-grade quality without having to manage model downloads or worry about APK size bloat. Your app also benefits automatically from hardware acceleration across NPU and TPU backends (when available) and seamless background model updates.

Integrating ASR and TTS into cross-platform applications usually requires handling low-level audio framing, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and complex decoding pipelines. MediaPipe Task simplifies this by providing unified, turnkey ASR and TTS APIs across iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, and Web that abstract away manual pre-processing, audio stream routing, and platform-specific audio management into simple, high-level interfaces:

Under the hood, ML Kit and MediaPipe Tasks are powered by LiteRT, Google’s high-performance on-device AI inference infrastructure. Cross-platform applications requiring even more fine-grained control over speech processing or custom model architectures can also build on it directly.

Speech models often rely on multiple subgraphs and auxiliary assets, such as encoder/decoder subgraphs and tokenizers for ASR, or phonemizer dictionaries, voice embeddings, and vocoders for TTS. All required components for each model are packaged into a single .litertlm file for easy deployment. The app ships with ready-to-use .litertlm models, including Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (multilingual ASR), PocketTTS 100M (multilingual TTS), Phonon 31M (ultra-lightweight English TTS), and Kokoro-82M (multilingual TTS). Beyond these, the vibrant Hugging Face LiteRT Community with over 10K+ followers offers a growing catalog of open-weight models, like Whisper, Qwen3-ASR and Moonshine for ASR, or Qwen3-TTS and Matcha for TTS. For developers seeking custom implementations or support for additional open-weight voice models, LiteRT provides a rich set of multimodal model examples to help you get started, with more on the way.

Adding a local voice pipeline takes on-device SLMs beyond typing-based chat interfaces, enabling natural, voice-first interactions that work anywhere, completely offline. All the building blocks to try these experiences or integrate them into your own apps are available today:

We'd like to extend a special thanks to our significant contributors for their work on this project:

#9877. Anthropic's super bug-finding Mythos model is going into Cisco and IBM products

Enterprise security tools will offer its capabilities without handing customers the model itself

Anthropic has started extending access to its bug-finding Mythos model by allowing Cisco and IBM to make it part of their security products.

Cisco announced its integration today at an event in Melbourne, Australia, where it revealed that the red teaming tools in its AI Defense suite, which looks for weaknesses and inappropriate activity in AI models, agents, and applications they power, will be able to call Mythos to test customers’ setups.

“At a very high level, AI Defense has the ability to look at models and break them,” said Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing. He said the tool is now “super-charged by Mythos” and will identify more danger that AI Defense will then address.

AI Defense already uses AI-powered red teaming to find flaws. Mythos will become another option. Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost.

Natalie Mead, Anthropic’s head of applied AI for the Asia-Pacific, said the company has a long queue of buyers who want to use Mythos, and working with Cisco will make it easier to satisfy that demand.

Anthropic initially made Mythos available under "Project Glasswing," a program that gave vetted organizations access to the model to test their codebases, but has since expanded access through other controlled programs, an arrangement that makes considerable sense because in the wrong hands Mythos could help attackers exploit software flaws.

The Cisco deal exposes the functionality of Mythos to end-users, without letting them use the model itself.

The Register asked Mead if Anthropic has similar deals with other third parties and she demurred. That may be because a few hours after Cisco told us about its use of Mythos, IBM announced that it will also integrate Anthropic’s model into a product – namely its Concert tool, which uses AI to scan applications for risks and weaknesses.

IBM says it will use Mythos “to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.”

We have asked Anthropic if these integrations represent a decision to open Mythos to more users in more ways. We will update this story if we receive a substantial response.

Also on Monday, Anthropic introduced version 5.2 of Mythos and Fable, which the company says generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than version 5.1 yet cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Users can choose to run both models in “fast mode,” which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times, and doubles prices to $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Anthropic says it “ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes.”

After those tests, the company concluded “high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures.

“Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.”

The latter is a telling admission, given Anthropic believes Chinese AI labs use distillation to effectively clone its models without doing expensive training work. ®

#9876. Two apps one process

So what if you can handle thousands of concurrent users per core? Even the front page of HN gets you what? 100 concurrent users on a good day?

Exactly! Most successful apps have like what 10 or 20 concurrent users at any given time? This is basically academic for most projects. What does performance give you other than knowing that your app won't need to scale past a single server? Pointless!

Well what if you could run multiple apps in one process?

Isn't that the same as a bunch of apps behind a reverse proxy?

No. It's not. Separate processes have to compete for OS resources, have their own thread pools, schedulers, heap, GC, caches and so on. Each process needs to be sized relative to the other apps running on the system.

But, in a single process you can size the process for the machine and then run an arbitrary number of apps in that process. If the apps share a process, they can share all sorts of things: a single JVM, GC, caches, buffers, http server, HTTPS certificate management, batching, game loop etc. You'd eliminate thread contention between apps. This lets you scale further with less resources!

Performance lets you run as many apps as you want in that one process.

Disclaimer: all my writing and code is handcrafted by me. By the end of this you may wish it wasn't.

If you have multiple JVMs you duplicate a bunch of fixed costs:

If you have multiple HTTP servers you duplicate:

If you have multiple framework engines you duplicate:

All of this adds up to more memory, more threads and more contention. If you own all your app and don't need the isolation a processes give you, then it can be a big performance win to have one JVM, one http server, and one framework engine.

X * n where X is you fixed cost for the above and n is your number of apps. If all of the above takes 500MB, then four apps is an extra 1.5GB.

Indeed. If you think about it an app at it's simplest is a domain, a database and some routes.

But, my reverse proxy handles HTTPS certs and stuff! Where is your god now?

Yes certs are a pain. But Clave: Automatic HTTPS certificate management and renewal via ACME, implemented in pure Clojure with minimal dependencies exists. I use it with aleph. But, it also works with jetty and it's simple to extend to other servers.

To bundle our apps we import them as dependencies into a separate project who's only purpose is to configure and start the server.

So adding a new app is as simple as importing it and adding it to the list of apps:

We can then build this project as an uberjar and scp it to the server.

Well this is nice and all, but whenever you deploy an app, you restart the process. DOWNTIME! UNACCEPTABLE!

Here's a gif of me deploying the jar to production:

If a deploy is indistinguishable from network blip did the app really go down?

That's it. We've reduced the overhead and cost of deploying a new app to zero.

Code can be found here. All three apps are running on the same JVM, on the same 10$ VPS , here, here and here.

#9875. From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in one click

Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate quickly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

“At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI

With the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a new domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

When selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

On the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

You’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

You arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

Alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

The launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

#9874. What's new in Node.js 27

Node.js 27 brings V8 15.6 with Iterator.zip, Iterator.zipKeyed, Math.sumPrecise, net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, and a 4 GB default heap limit.

On October 29, 2026, the Node.js team published v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0. If you have been using Node.js for a few years, that version string alone probably made you do a double take. Where is the usual October v27.0.0 Current release?

Node.js 27 is the first release to follow the new annual schedule. Under the old schedule, October brought a major release that reached end of life six months later without entering Long Term Support (LTS). October now starts a six-month Alpha phase, ahead of the 27.0.0 Current release in April 2027 and LTS promotion in October 2027.

Wait, an odd-numbered Node.js release becoming LTS?

Yes, the odd/even split is gone. Version numbers now match the calendar year (27 in 2027), with one major release per year, and every release becomes LTS. We covered the timeline and the reasons for the change in Node.js is changing its release schedule and version numbers. Because Node.js 27 is currently in its Alpha window, I will keep updating this article as new builds land on the way to April 2027.

In this first Alpha, V8 moves from 14.6 to 15.6, adding Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), and Math.sumPrecise(). There is a promises API for node:net, along with async-iterable TCP servers. The Virtual File System (node:vfs) is now unflagged, the Permission Model gains --allow-env, and HTTP and memory defaults change too.

We’ll start with the JavaScript and Node.js APIs you can use in everyday code, comparing them with the older approaches. Then we’ll cover runtime changes and what to check before upgrading.

Every code block with a file path in its title matches a runnable file in the companion repo lmammino/nodejs-27-examples on GitHub.

For example, we can format a list of products and total their prices:

If you want to experiment locally, check your current Node.js version before running the snippets below.

This is the part of the release I’m most excited about. I love seeing how far we can push streams, iterators, and generators. Our article on JavaScript async iterators should give you an idea of what I mean.

In What’s new in Node.js 26, we used Iterator.concat() to consume multiple iterables one after another. Node.js 27, through V8 15.6, lets us consume them side by side, pairing values at the same position.

Suppose you are checking a weather forecast against the temperatures recorded over the same four days. The predictions come from your model, while the actual values come from observations. To calculate each day’s error, you need to pair the values at the same position. Both sequences must cover the same days in the same order.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, if both sequences were arrays, you would typically use .map() with an index lookup:

That works well for arrays. But what if observations come from a generator, or your model returns an iterator of predictions? Index lookups won’t work on those inputs, and converting them to arrays means loading both sequences into memory first.

In Node.js 27, Iterator.zip() takes an iterable of iterables and returns a lazy iterator of pairs. We can calculate the errors with the same pipeline whether the inputs are arrays or iterators:

Each pair contains a prediction and its corresponding observation. A positive error means the day was warmer than predicted; a negative error means it was cooler. The pairing and mapping happen one item at a time. Only the final .toArray() collects the errors into an array so we can print them together.

Another common use is the dot product of two vectors: multiply matching components, then add the products. This operation appears in graphics, machine learning, and numerical computing:

Here we never collect the pairs or products into an intermediate array. We also use mode: 'strict' because a dot product requires vectors of equal length: silently ignoring extra components would hide an input error.

By default, Iterator.zip() uses { mode: 'shortest' }: it stops when the shortest input finishes and closes the remaining open iterators. For the forecast example, that means comparing only the days available in both sequences. Use { mode: 'strict' } if a missing prediction or observation should instead throw a TypeError. Or pass { mode: 'longest', padding: [null, 0] } to continue until the longest input finishes, using the corresponding padding value when an input runs out.

So far, our inputs have been arrays. But Iterator.zip() also works with iterators that have no end. Imagine a home with two power meters: one measures solar generation, and the other measures household consumption. Each meter gives us its current reading in watts whenever we poll it. Subtracting consumption from generation tells us whether the house has surplus power to export or needs to import power from the grid (assuming there is no battery).

We can wrap each meter in an endless generator. Here we simulate the readings with random values so the example runs without hardware:

Neither generator reads anything until we request a value from netPower. Each request polls both meters once and calculates the difference. Both input iterators can keep producing readings forever, but .take(5) limits this demo to five pairs. Collecting either input with [...solar] or .toArray() would never finish and would eventually exhaust memory.

These are synchronous, on-demand readings: the two meters are polled sequentially, close together, rather than at exactly the same instant. The loop takes five readings immediately; zip() does not add a polling interval. With real hardware, the callbacks would read the meters instead of generating random numbers.

Tuple arrays like [prediction, observation] are easy to read for two or three items, but once you have four or five parallel sources, positional destructuring gets easy to mix up.

Iterator.zipKeyed() accepts an object whose values are iterables. Each step yields an object with the same keys, so you can refer to values by name instead of position:

If an API returns each field as a separate array, like user IDs, names, and roles, Iterator.zipKeyed() lets you process them together as a lazy sequence of row objects. The arrays must describe the same records in the same order.

In Node.js 26, a common way to format a lazy iterator pipeline as a string was to call .toArray().join(', ') at the end. The final .toArray() allocated an array of strings that .join() consumed and discarded.

V8 15.6 adds two terminal helpers directly onto Iterator.prototype:

For join(), let’s return to our sensor readings. This time we only need one temperature sensor, and we want to format five readings as a comma-separated string. As before, we simulate the hardware so you can run the example locally:

.take(5) makes the endless source finite, .map() formats each reading, and .join() builds the string without collecting an intermediate array. These five readings are taken immediately, with no delay between them. Without .take(5), joining this endless iterator would never finish.

For includes(), imagine checking whether a commit message references a particular issue. String.prototype.matchAll() already returns an iterator, so we can extract the complete references and search them directly:

includes() stops as soon as it finds APP-142, without extracting the later reference. Matching complete references also avoids the false positive you would get from message.includes('APP-14'), which matches part of APP-142. The search consumes the iterator, so create a fresh one for another search.

The iterator helpers shown above work with synchronous iterators. Their .next() calls return results directly; these helpers do not await promises from async iterators. You cannot use the same chains on an async function* generator or a Node.js readable stream’s async iterator. Use for await...of or a library with async iterator helpers for those sources. Async iterator helpers are covered by a separate TC39 proposal and are not built into Node.js 27 as of v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0.

Beyond iterator helpers, V8 15.6 also brings a useful addition for numerical calculations: Math.sumPrecise(). To see why it matters, let’s look at a familiar floating-point surprise.

When you sum numbers with .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0), each addition rounds its intermediate result to the nearest representable 64-bit float. Over dozens or thousands of additions, those tiny rounding errors accumulate. Worse, if you add a small number (0.1) to a huge number (1e20) and later add -1e20, the 0.1 is lost completely during the first addition because a 64-bit float doesn’t have enough mantissa bits to hold both magnitudes at once.

In Node.js 27, V8 15.6 enables Math.sumPrecise() by default. It accepts any iterable of numbers, computes the sum using an internal high-precision accumulator, and rounds only once at the very end:

Math.sumPrecise() accepts any iterable, so it also works with the iterators from the previous section. You can pass the result of .map() directly into Math.sumPrecise() without calling .toArray() first:

When you still need integer cents or decimal libraries

Math.sumPrecise() avoids rounding after each addition. Its result is what you would get by adding the exact mathematical values of the input floating-point numbers, then rounding the total once to the nearest representable 64-bit float. But those inputs may already differ from the decimal values you intended:

As the MDN explanation points out, the literals 0.1 and 0.2 are stored as binary floating-point values slightly greater than their exact decimal counterparts. Adding those stored values and rounding once still produces 0.30000000000000004. The method cannot recover the intended decimal inputs.

For money calculations that require exact decimal arithmetic, use integer minor units (like cents) or a decimal library with explicit rounding rules. Math.sumPrecise() improves summation accuracy; it does not turn JavaScript numbers into decimal numbers.

The core node:net module gets iterator support too.

For years, node:fs, node:dns, node:stream, node:timers, and node:readline have all had .promises sub-modules. Yet node:net remained purely callback- and event-driven. If you wanted to spin up a TCP server on an ephemeral port in a test or connect a client socket using async/await, you had to wrap 'listening', 'connect', and 'error' events by hand.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, setting up a TCP server and client with async/await looked like this:

Node.js 27 introduces the experimental node:net/promises module with two helpers, listen() and connect(), and makes net.Server itself an async iterable.

Let’s try something fun and build a small TCP chat server. Each connected client can send a line of text, and the server forwards it to every other client, prefixed with the sender’s connection ID:

Then open two or three other terminals and run this command in each (with netcat installed):

Each terminal receives its connection ID, for example Connected as 127.0.0.1:54321. Type a message and press Enter. The other terminals receive a line such as 127.0.0.1:54321 > Hello everyone!. The server does not echo messages back to their sender. Press Ctrl+C in a client terminal to disconnect, or in the server terminal to close the chat and all active connections.

With three netcat clients connected, each terminal receives the other clients’ messages:

listen() resolves once the server is listening. The clients map tracks active sockets by their remote address and port, which distinguish connections to this server. These are connection labels, not permanent user identities: reconnecting can give a client a different port.

Inside each handler, readline turns the socket’s byte stream into lines. TCP chunks do not correspond to messages: a line may arrive in several chunks, or one chunk may contain several lines. Each completed line is broadcast to every other active socket. The finally block removes disconnected clients and closes their resources.

The outer connection loop starts each handleConnection(socket) call without awaiting it. That lets it accept the next client while earlier handlers wait for messages. Each handler still awaits its own incoming lines, so clients can remain connected and chat concurrently. The .catch() handles rejected handler promises; socket errors are handled separately, and server.maxConnections = 10 caps open connections for this demo.

The pitfall: awaiting each connection handler

This small change would break the chat’s concurrency:

handleConnection() stays active until its client disconnects. Awaiting it here means only the first client gets a handler and joins the clients map. Later connections can be accepted by the server, but the loop will not dispatch their handlers until that first client leaves. There is nobody else in the map to receive the first client’s messages!

The server iterator documentation warns that a slow consumer can buffer connections without bound. Set server.maxConnections explicitly and choose a limit appropriate to your workload, including when dispatching handlers concurrently.

The iterator yields TCP connections, not individual chat messages or application-level requests. Awaiting a handler can be appropriate for deliberate sequential processing, but a chat server needs overlapping connection handlers.

Testing code that reads configuration files often means mocking node:fs or creating temporary directories and cleaning them up afterward. Bundling assets or templates into an archive poses a related problem: how can your application read them through its usual node:fs calls?

The new node:vfs (Virtual File System) module was originally introduced behind --experimental-vfs, and in Node.js 27 it is unflagged and available out of the box (though still marked Experimental Stability 1 while the API settles).

With node:vfs, you can create an isolated, in-memory file system with vfs.create(), populate it using standard fs-style methods, and mount it so regular node:fs operations (and import / require()) can read from it directly. VirtualFileSystem also supports Explicit Resource Management (using), which unmounts it when execution leaves the block:

The using declaration tells JavaScript to call memoryFs[Symbol.dispose]() when execution leaves the block, including when an error is thrown. VirtualFileSystem implements that method to unmount itself. Declaring it with const would require us to call unmount() explicitly.

memoryFs.mount() mounts the virtual file system under a reserved namespace (path.join(os.devNull, 'vfs'), such as /dev/null/vfs/1 on POSIX), so a virtual mount can never accidentally shadow or overwrite real files on your disk. If you want to compare this with working on real files, check out our guide on reading and writing files in Node.js.

You can also use node:vfs through --vfs-load on the CLI without an experimental flag:

That command mounts the companion repo’s 04-vfs/bundle directory and runs its index.js, which prints Hello from the VFS bundle. You can also pass a ZIP archive; Node.js runs its package.json "main" or index.js entry point from the mounted archive. And if you use Single Executable Applications (SEA), vfsArchive is now mounted at layer 0 and automatically available inside Worker threads too.

There are changes across the standard library too, from temporary files to HTTP server defaults.

Until now, if you needed a temporary file in Node.js, your safest built-in option was fs.mkdtemp() to create a temporary directory, and then opening a file inside it. Creating a random filename yourself and calling fs.open() was error-prone and required a retry loop in case of collisions.

Node.js 27 adds APIs modeled on POSIX mkstemp(3): fs.mkstemp(), fs.mkstempSync(), and fsPromises.mkstemp(). It atomically generates a unique filename (appending six random characters to your prefix) and opens the file in a single step, returning both the path and the open FileHandle (or file descriptor fd):

The built-in fs.glob() (introduced in Node.js 22) was ported from JavaScript to native C++ in Node.js 27. The maintainers’ benchmarks show substantial speedups for some workloads, but gains vary by API and options, and one synchronous exclude-pattern workload regressed. Benchmark your own patterns before assuming a speedup.

As we covered in our guide to environment variables in Node.js, process.env is where most applications keep their most sensitive secrets (API keys, database URLs, signing tokens). It is also the very first place a compromised dependency looks when trying to exfiltrate credentials.

Node.js 27 adds --allow-env to the Permission Model (--permission). When --permission is enabled, every environment variable not explicitly matched by --allow-env is scrubbed at process startup before any JavaScript runs (except runtime variables like PATH, HOME, LANG, and NODE_OPTIONS, plus variables explicitly loaded via --env-file):

Node.js also scrubs disallowed variables from the underlying OS environment block and restricts access to /proc/self/environ on Linux. Native code loaded by Node.js sees the reduced environment too. This reduces accidental exposure; the Permission Model is not a sandbox for malicious code. You can remove a variable after reading it with process.permission.drop('env', 'VARIABLE_NAME'). Keep NODE_ENV explicitly if your application uses it, since it is not preserved by default.

The built-in node:test runner has three updates:

These three HTTP changes affect production web servers:

If you are curious why this change was made: it seems a bit weird on the surface, right? Why would Node.js remove the prototype from an otherwise ordinary object?

req.headers is a dictionary: the keys are header names chosen by whoever sent the request, and the values are whatever they sent. An ordinary JavaScript object is a poor fit for that kind of data, because it inherits properties from Object.prototype that have nothing to do with what you stored in it:

Our empty ordinary object already “has” a constructor, inherited from its prototype. __proto__ is even more surprising: Object.prototype defines an accessor with that name, so reading it returns the prototype, and assigning to it tries to change the prototype instead of storing a value. Both names are already lowercase, which matters here because Node.js lowercases incoming header names. A client can send a constructor or __proto__ header, and it arrives under exactly that key.

Notice that the example uses __proto__ in two different ways. { __proto__: null } is special object-literal syntax that creates the object with no prototype at all (Object.create(null) does the same thing, and the new Node.js code uses the literal form). The later headers['__proto__'] = ... is an ordinary assignment: with no inherited __proto__ setter to intercept it, it simply stores an own property, like any other key.

That’s the motivation in PR #62900, by Matteo Collina. Besides consistency with the *Distinct APIs, its commit message says the change “Fixes prototype pollution concerns where headers like __proto__ could be interpreted as prototype manipulation.” My reading is that the goal is clean dictionary semantics: a key exists in req.headers only if the request sent it.

The March 2026 security releases already included a real bug of this kind. CVE-2026-21710 was a denial-of-service flaw in req.headersDistinct, and it went like this:

Because the exception is thrown synchronously inside a property getter, an 'error' event listener can’t catch it. The fix initialized the headersDistinct and trailersDistinct objects with { __proto__: null }, which is the behavior PR #62900 later extended to headers and trailers. The advisory covers headersDistinct only, so it doesn’t mean req.headers had the same crash. The bug also stopped at crashing the process: a header couldn’t use it to modify Object.prototype globally. And a null-prototype object removes inherited-property hazards only where the headers are created. If you merge headers into an ordinary object, that target still has the inherited __proto__ accessor.

Node.js 27 also updates its engine and bundled dependencies. Most of the V8 details below come from Joyee Cheung’s Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha) on the Node.js blog, which is worth reading in full if you maintain performance-sensitive code or native tooling:

Default Heap Limit up to 4 GB on mid-sized machines: When --max-old-space-size is not specified, V8 now sets the default old-generation heap limit to half of physical memory (or container cgroup memory), clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB. Previously, machines with less than 15 GB of RAM were capped at 2 GB. On an 8 GB container or VM, the default old-generation limit therefore rises from 2 GB to 4 GB (and on a 6 GB machine, from 2 GB to 3 GB). These are old-generation limits, not limits on the process’s total memory use.

Buffer and ArrayBuffer memory affects garbage collection scheduling: Memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances is now included in V8’s global allocation limit. If your app allocates large off-heap buffers (for example, image processing or large file buffers), this affects when garbage collection is scheduled. The global allocation limit is distinct from the old-generation heap limit and does not impose a hard cap on the process’s total memory.

Slightly more memory per worker and per native object: Each V8 isolate (the main thread and every worker thread) uses about 180 KB more for property lookup caches, and every JavaScript object that wraps a native resource (a socket, file handle, stream, hash, or blob) may use about 16 bytes more on the heap and about 50 bytes more outside it. That’s negligible for most apps, but it adds up if you spawn many workers or hold many open sockets.

Fewer hard crashes on fatal errors: More fatal V8 errors now go through Node.js’s fatal error handling before aborting, so --report-on-fatalerror can produce a diagnostic report in cases that previously aborted without one. Some extreme inputs (overly long template literals, classes with too many elements, a regexp too large to compile) now throw a RangeError instead of crashing the process. The V8 post is explicit that this isn’t guaranteed, so don’t build program logic around it.

These numbers come from V8’s own benchmarks, and the impact varies with platform, workload, and build configuration. Measure your application before counting on a speedup.

OpenSSL 4.1.0, Undici 8.12, SQLite 3.54, and npm 12.1.0: Node.js 27 upgrades its bundled cryptography to OpenSSL 4.1.0, strips out all legacy OpenSSL 1.x compatibility shims and engine APIs, bumps npm to 12.1.0, and updates NODE_MODULE_VERSION to 153.

The Alpha window gives you time to check for breaking changes before the stable release. Most applications won’t encounter all of these, but check your code and dependencies for the following changes.

As we saw in the HTTP section, the header dictionaries no longer have a prototype. Normal property access (req.headers['content-type']), destructuring, and Object.keys() work as before. What breaks is calling methods inherited from Object.prototype: req.headers.hasOwnProperty('authorization') now throws a TypeError (and calling a method looked up on a dictionary of external data was never a good idea anyway).

Replace it with Object.hasOwn(req.headers, 'authorization'), which doesn’t rely on the object’s prototype and works on both Node.js 26 and 27. Please don’t “fix” this by restoring Object.prototype on the headers object. The in operator still works on null-prototype objects, but the updated Node.js docs advise against using it here, and Object.hasOwn() expresses the own-property check you actually mean.

This runnable example shows both the failure and the fix. Keep in mind that checking for a header’s presence does not authenticate its value:

If you run multiple Node.js processes on a 6 GB or 8 GB machine and relied on the old implicit 2 GB heap cap to keep them from starving each other, pass --max-old-space-size=2048 explicitly. Similarly, if your application holds hundreds of megabytes of Buffer data in memory alongside a large JS heap, be aware that Buffer allocations now influence V8’s global allocation limit and garbage collection scheduling.

Most V8 changes are invisible, but a few can break code that depends on exact results:

The V8 changes post lists more edge cases, including fractional getTimezoneOffset() values for historical dates and stricter take()/drop() limits on iterators.

When testing your project or library against Node.js 27:

For production, the release date matters. For library authors and local experiments, there is already code to try:

If you want to install the Alpha side by side with your stable LTS runtime without messing up your system setup, check out our guide on 5 ways to install Node.js using version managers like fnm or nvm.

Want to write modern, production-ready Node.js?

Our book Node.js Design Patterns covers streams, iterators, async control flow, modules, and scalable architectures. The runtime changes each year; these patterns help you design applications across releases.

Node.js 27 starts the annual release schedule, with every major version going on to LTS. Its first Alpha includes V8 15.6, node:net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, fs.mkstemp(), and --allow-env.

I’d start by trying Iterator.zipKeyed() and Iterator.prototype.join() in a data-transformation script. They let you process parallel collections lazily without collecting intermediate arrays.

For the full list of commits and low-level details, check out the official Node.js 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 release notes and the companion post on Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha).

Thanks to the Node.js releasers, V8 maintainers, and contributors who worked on this first Alpha and the new release schedule.

Node.js 27 is the first version under the new Node.js release schedule. Instead of two major releases per year, Node.js now ships one major release every April, preceded by a six-month Alpha testing phase starting in October.

Yes. Under the new release schedule, the old odd/even rule is gone and every yearly major release becomes LTS. Node.js 27 will enter Current in April 2027, move to LTS in October 2027, and be supported until April 2030.

Thanks to V8 15.6, Node.js 27 ships Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), Math.sumPrecise(), and Intl.Locale.prototype.variants enabled by default.

When --max-old-space-size is not set, V8 now defaults to half of physical memory clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB (meaning an 8 GB machine gets a 4 GB heap instead of 2 GB). Additionally, memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances now counts toward V8’s global allocation limit, affecting when garbage collection runs.

If you are reading this before April 2027, keep production workloads on an LTS release. Node.js 27 is still in its Alpha testing phase during that period, intended for library authors, CI pipelines, and experimentation. It is scheduled to enter Current in April 2027 and LTS in October 2027. Once a stable release is available, evaluate it against your application’s support requirements.

#9873. Cisco to link all future products to its SaaS-y Cloud Control management tool

Global rollout of unified portal finally happening in 2027

Cisco will no longer create products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control, its SaaS-y management platform that offers netadmins a single tool to manage all of the networking giant’s devices and much of its software portfolio.

It appears Cisco is now satisfied it has sorted out those issues. Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing, today told the company’s Live conference in Australia that Cloud Control will come online in the European Union, UK, and Down Under in February 2027. Japan, India, and Canada will get their turn in May.

Schultz said Cisco is “working tirelessly” to deploy Cloud Control across the world as soon as possible.

He also revealed that, starting next year, Cisco will no longer ship products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control.

That doesn’t mean those products will be manageable only if they can connect to Cloud Control. Instead, the decision reflects Cisco’s belief that the main thing stopping its customers buying more of its products is the complexity of operating them in concert. Schultz also feels that Cloud Control represents “platform advantage” for Cisco, because when users integrate networking, security, and observability the result is better manageability and resilience.

Schultz also told the conference that Cisco will bundle its Thousand Eyes observability and security tool with the “Essentials” and “Advantage” licenses. “We admit it was hard to license and deploy,” he said during his keynote speech, adding that the tool will be deployed automatically with Wi‑Fi 6E and Wi‑Fi 7 hardware.

Another product Cisco plans to bring to more customers is Live Protect, a tool that implements compensating controls for flaws that organizations can’t immediately patch. The product has become particularly useful since Anthropic's Mythos model, and similar AI offerings, made it possible to quickly find more software bugs and flaws and overwhelmed tech teams whose patching apparatus was not set up to handle hundreds of montly CVEs.

Live Protect currently works on some of Cisco's datacenter switches, plus SD-WAN and WLAN controllers. From December, Cisco will extend it to 8000 series routers, secure firewalls, campus gateway, and to Cloud Control itself. From May 2027, Live Protect will work with Cisco’s ASR 9000 series service aggregation routers and Network Convergence System.

"Expect this to be a major investment area," Schultz added. ®

#9872. Native-speed vLLM transformers modeling backend

TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures. Model authors can automatically leverage their transformers implementations to get ultra fast vLLM inference, for free.

The transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning. It supports 450+ architectures through consistent APIs, and is designed with the main goal that model implementations are self contained and easy to understand. Going through transformers code makes it easy for contributors to learn how an architecture works, and then port it to other frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, llama.cpp, and many others.

We have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier. A big step in this direction was the integration last year of transformers as a modeling backend in vLLM. This has been allowing model authors to run transformers models (LLMs and VLMs alike) inside vLLM, without having to port anything. Transformers provides the modeling code, and vLLM provides extremely optimized inference techniques such as continuous batching and custom attention kernels.

We put the transformers modeling backend for vLLM head to head with vLLM's hand written native implementations across three very different Qwen3 models:

Running any* Hugging Face model through the transformers modeling backend is a single flag — --model-impl transformers. It composes with the usual parallelism options, so nothing about your serving setup changes:

*Models that use linear attention are not currently supported, but they will be soon! Custom models where the code lives in a Hub repo are unlikely to work as they will not have been written compliantly.

Each model is compared under three conditions that are identical in every way except the code path:

The full, reproducible runner is available as a gist: benchmark.sh

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM used to focus on attention as the bottleneck for inference. By plugging vLLM’s attention implementation at runtime, we could make a transformers model run efficiently inside the vLLM engine. But there are many dimensions to deployments that only a custom port can target to extract maximum inference performance. Parallelization across GPUs, compilation, fused kernels, and many more, all contribute to leveraging your hardware to achieve ultra-fast inference.

When model authors wanted the absolute best performance, they were still writing custom vLLM implementations.

The latest iteration of the transformers modeling backend for vLLM dynamically applies inference specific layer fusions at runtime to match the speed of custom code implementations, for compatible architectures.

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM now uses torch.fx to perform static analysis on the model’s graph. This process searches for known patterns that can be optimised. After any patterns have been identified, it uses ast (abstract syntax tree) to manipulate the source code and rewrite some of the operations in place.

As shown above, this results in native vLLM inference speed for compatible models, without having to write a single line of code to optimize the model for inference.

We are in the process of writing a detailed blog post to dive deep inside these optimized inference methods and explain in detail how we manipulate the model to adapt to them.

One provenance implication here is that the model definition and the executed inference graph are no longer the same artifact boundary.

If the runtime rewrites model code and replaces modules with fused kernels, deployment evidence probably needs to preserve both the source model identity and the transformation/runtime path.

#9870. Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild

Tom Ritter1, Fatih Kilic2, Frederik Braun1, Elisa Luo3, Geoffrey M. Voelker3, Stefan Savage3, Christoph Kerschbaumer1

1Mozilla Corporation  ·  2University of Toronto  ·  3UC San Diego

Web browser fingerprinting has become a key tracking mechanism on the modern web, yet its real-world effectiveness and which of the existing mitigations offer value at scale remain insufficiently understood.

In this paper, we present a large-scale study of browser fingerprinting based on real-world telemetry from almost 25 million Firefox release users. This dataset enables us to quantify user uniqueness at population scale and identify which characteristics contribute most to this uniqueness.

Our analysis shows fingerprintability is largely driven by a small set of high-impact characteristics and their combinations, rather than the accumulation of many independent measurements. Building on these insights, we propose and evaluate fingerprinting protections based on their impact on uniqueness and cohort structure, and design data-driven mitigations.

These protections, shipped in Firefox 143, reduce the fraction of uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46% while maintaining web compatibility, demonstrating that practical reductions in fingerprintability are achievable in a mainstream browser.

Here's what we want to present to you with this paper and the broader scope of our work.

Fingerprinting test sites have a seemingly endless list of measurements they can pull from your browser. If a user has a unique fingerprint, it is typically not because of a single measurement, but it is also not because of 20 or 30 measurements. It is a small number of metrics that make users unique.

In fact, it's very close to the 80/20 rule. Specifically, of all the users seen as unique by Fingerprint Pro (the most discerning fingerprinter we model) - 80% of them are unique after only 8 metrics - while the fingerprinter collects a total of over 50 metrics. Signifyd collects more metrics, but identifies fewer users as unique: 80% of the users it sees as unique will be identified after 9 metrics despite collecting over 80.

Whenever someone cites a single percentage when describing "How many users are unique" - you should be suspicious. Because this collapses multiple different populations that behave very differently.

Firstly, as a baseline, your operating system is always going to be exposed to a fingerprinter. We are always working within the constraint of web compatibility, and lying about the user's operating system breaks shortcut keys and gives you the wrong downloads among other problems. So if we know the website is going to learn your real OS anyway, we can use it to segment the population and analyze it separately.

And when you do you see that each operating system behaves differently because they have different important metrics. Admittedly, it's very difficult to give a concise summary of work and also provide four sets of numbers - so even we fall prey to the trap of providing a single number, as we did in the prior paragraph. But every time we have a single percentage, somewhere we have that number broken down by operating system, and in doing so, you will see that each behaves differently.

It's so, so easy to take all the results for a metric and just calculate Shannon entropy - it's a standard yardstick in this literature. But as we show - a high Shannon entropy does not reliably predict fingerprinting impact.

Previous analyses calculated how many people were unique, but they did not analyze the other people - the ones who weren't. All those other people might be 1 million users who share one fingerprint or 500,000 distinct fingerprints shared by 2 people each - that's quite the difference.

We use the Simpson Index (aka the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index) to quantify that difference and compare different sets of cohorts (shared fingerprints). This lets us compare how effective different fingerprinting defenses are based not just on how much uniqueness they eliminate but how much they collapse groups of users into each other.

For example, two different protections can each lower the share of unique users by about 2.1 percentage points. But one improves the cohort score by 56%, while another raises it by only 13%. Judged on uniqueness alone, two defenses can look equally effective; while the cohort improvement varies significantly.

Protections are not uniformly impactful, and the variation is not small. As an example, clamping the available screen resolution takes 25.3 percentage points off cumulative macOS uniqueness but between 0 and 3 points off the other three platforms. Averaged across all users, that 25-point drop shrinks to 3.5 - a protection that matters enormously to one platform can look marginal in the aggregate.

This is yet another reason why it's so important to segment and analyze data on a per-operating-system basis.

Correlating fingerprinting values with users' hardware and other characteristics let us identify why certain measurements differed between users. Knowing the root cause lets us build protections that reach much further, and protect small groups of users who would otherwise stand out as a minority.

Addressing these differences has already produced more consistent outputs for image rendering, Web Audio, and mathematical operations on Android, with more root causes being investigated.

Breakage from a strict mode is delayed, and the delay hides the cause. Turning on a stricter mode is a one-time act - but the broken website arrives later and nothing connects the two. From the user's perspective, this website doesn't work in Firefox and they have no idea why and are frustrated. Report after report we see people posting for help, confused - despite having taken specific action to enable a hidden setting opting them into strict fingerprinting protections.

The web is vast, and even the most innocuous change is likely to break something somewhere. Some breakage can be anticipated, which helps design, testing, and detection. The other breakage gets fixed only if a chain of luck holds: someone has to recognize the breakage, report it, reproduce it on the right hardware, and get it to the right person.

Commercial fingerprinters evolve continuously, and they borrow openly from the community that studies them. Sites built to teach people about fingerprinting - CreepJS among them - get picked up and used outright by fingerprinting products.

So we have been deliberately conservative. There are analyses this dataset would support that we have not run, data we could have released that we have not, and offensive angles on this work that we have not pursued. That is a choice rather than an oversight: we would rather leave a question open than make it easier to build a better fingerprinter.

This interactive test re-implements individual measurements as close as possible to how Firefox's own collection code performed them, runs in your browser, and compares each result against the published aggregate data. For every characteristic you can see your value and how many of the ~25 million measured browsers share it - overall and within your operating system.

The test runs entirely in your browser. All comparisons happen locally, against our static reference files. No data is stored or submitted to us.

If the test, or anything else on this site, looks wrong, please report it as an issue on GitHub. For a problem with the test, include the diagnostics from its Copy diagnostics button, or, if you would rather not post your measured values publicly, email them to tom@ritter.vg.

The extended version of the paper is available as a PDF.

The paper's appendices contain a wealth of data locked behind a reasonable page limit and PDF formatting. This full data page carries all of it - every rank for every operating system and all three modeled services, the complete protection chains, and the paper's figures regenerated at print resolution.

Our measurements come from Firefox telemetry, specifically the user-characteristics ping, a dedicated telemetry ping. Unlike normal telemetry pings that are sent regularly, this ping must be explicitly enabled (which has happened twice, once in 2025 and once in 2026), and sends one data report before becoming dormant again.

This ping carries no client ID, only a UUID unique to the ping used to de-duplicate users. It cannot be keyed to any other telemetry submissions. It is submitted over Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP): a relay operated independently of Mozilla forwards the encrypted submission, so the relay can see the sender's IP address but not the contents, and Mozilla receives the contents but not the IP address. Access to the collected data was restricted to four authorized Mozilla employees. The data was retained for 90 days and has since been deleted.

In the fingerprint lists, the fingerprints cannot be recreated from a website measuring user characteristics, due to the way the telemetry was collected. After being generated, the files were shuffled to a new ordering, and any locale occurring fewer than 100 times was anonymized.

In the aggregate tables, any value observed fewer than 100 times within a single per-OS population is withheld - so the published data describes cohorts, never individuals.

In the canvas comparison, raw canvas renderings are provided, but they are devoid of any connection to other user data. Any unique canvas rendering is not provided; only the hash.

For verification and exploration, the code used to process the data and perform different analyses is available for review. It additionally contains the specific fingerprinting scripts captured, reverse engineered, and modeled for the paper.

Far more can be asked of this dataset than we have asked. Some of it we chose not to pursue, some of it we simply did not think of, and some of it is a better fit for someone who is not us.

There is a discussion board for proposing follow-up analyses. Two kinds are worth posting:

This Firefox telemetry collection is opt-out and carries no client identifier for this ping. See the paper for the full methodology and its limitations.

Found a bug on this site? Report it on GitHub.

#9869. Microsoft teaches schools that free email was just a phase

Office 365 A1 and Student Use Benefit face retirement, leaving institutions to budget for paid replacements at renewal

Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students' mailboxes.

The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028.

Office 365 A1 provides eligible institutions with web-based Office applications, Teams, and email at no charge. Its replacement, Microsoft 365 Education A0, excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also depends on paid faculty licensing and students actively using Windows devices for education.

A spokesperson for the UK's Department for Education told The Register: "We are disappointed that Microsoft has made this decision. However, we are pleased to have successfully negotiated some additional concessions for the UK, giving schools, colleges and universities the time they need to be able to successfully transition to new licensing agreements."

An industry insider said the loss of free Microsoft-hosted email could add thousands to institutions' bills. Another organization noted "significant concerns… around affordability, equitable treatment across the sector, and the longer-term implications of the changes."

A spokesperson for UK education technology body Jisc told The Register that its "focus has been on ensuring that UK education providers are well supported and have sufficient time to assess their options."

"We continue working closely with Microsoft and sector partners to support those discussions and help institutions make informed decisions about their future requirements."

Also being retired are free Exchange Online for Alumni – which lets graduates retain their mailboxes – and the Student Use Benefit, providing student licenses at no additional charge when institutions purchase qualifying faculty licenses. Microsoft plans a paid alumni replacement.

The Windows giant is also changing storage entitlements and introducing Microsoft 365 Education A7, its "most advanced education offering," which adds AI, security, governance, and device-management features.

Asked why it was removing those services from the free tier, Microsoft framed the overhaul as a response to institutions' changing needs.

"Microsoft is updating the portfolio now to provide a clearer path from foundational access to advanced capabilities, while enabling institutions to adopt technology according to their needs and readiness. This evolution reflects both the value Microsoft 365 Education has gained since the last pricing change nearly a decade ago and the structure of the new portfolio.

Office 365 A1 stopped accepting new web-direct orders on November 5, 2026, with partner-channel sales ending on May 1, 2027. Retirement is scheduled for January 1, 2028, but existing agreements remain valid through their current terms. Institutions that need continued service must move to replacement licenses at the applicable renewal or contract expiry. ®
